questions.prompt: What problem do actors solve, and how do they solve it?

expectedConcepts.text: Actors protect shared mutable state from concurrent access
Only one task executes actor-isolated code at a time
Isolation is enforced by the compiler, not by developer discipline
Cross-actor access is asynchronous and requires await

misconceptions.text: an actor blocks other callers like a lock
actors make code run on a background thread

modelAnswerOutline: Problem: shared mutable state accessed from multiple concurrent tasks causes data races.
An actor encapsulates its state and guarantees only one task touches it at a time.
The compiler enforces this: outside code cannot reach isolated state synchronously.
Access from outside is async, hence await, which is why it is not a lock.
Tradeoff: contention and actor hopping cost; isolate the state, not everything.

questions.prompt: Explain actor reentrancy. Why does it surprise people, and how do you defend against it?

expectedConcepts.text: An await inside an actor method suspends and lets other work run on the actor
State can change across the await, so assumptions made before it may be stale
Check-then-act sequences spanning an await are the classic bug
Defend by re-validating after the await, or by storing an in-flight task to deduplicate

misconceptions.text: an actor method runs atomically from start to finish
await inside an actor blocks other callers until it returns

modelAnswerOutline: Actor methods are not atomic: every await is a suspension point.
While suspended, another task can enter the actor and mutate state.
So anything read before the await may be stale after it.
Classic failure: `if cache[key] == nil { let v = await fetch(); cache[key] = v }` fetches twice.
Defenses: re-check state after resuming, or store the in-flight Task so callers await the same work.
